questions: B
Which structural feature makes template-directed DNA duplication possible?
Identical 5′→3′ sequences on both strands|Complementary base pairing between antiparallel strands|Covalent bonds between complementary bases|An invariant ratio of all four bases
B
Complementarity preserves positional information. The strands are reverse complements, not generally identical; their association is noncovalent, and equal base composition does not specify sequence.
B
After one complete light-medium round from HH DNA, which model predicts two extreme bands?
Semiconservative|Uniformly dispersive|Conservative|All three
C
Conservative copying retains the original HH duplex and makes LL. Both other ideal models yield intermediate density.
B
Which first-round observation alone cannot distinguish semiconservative and dispersive replication?
A single intermediate duplex band|Only heavy DNA|Equal heavy and light bands|No DNA synthesis
A
Both distribute half the ancestral material into each product, but differ in whether it remains an intact chain.
B
Which feature distinguishes the second-round semiconservative prediction?
A progressively shifting single band|One heavy band|A fixed intermediate band plus a light band|A fixed heavy band plus a hybrid band
C
The HL class retains its composition while LL products appear. A uniform dispersive model shifts toward light; conservative copying preserves HH.
B
The heavy isotope in the Meselson–Stahl experiment is:
A radioactive isotope of hydrogen|A stable nitrogen isotope|A radioactive isotope of nitrogen|A heavy isotope of phosphorus
B
Nitrogen-15 is stable. Tritium is radioactive hydrogen and was used in the chromosome-labeling experiment, not this density strategy.
B
At isopycnic equilibrium, a DNA molecule bands principally where:
Its length matches the tube radius|Its speed is greatest|The gradient contains no salt|Its effective buoyant density matches local solution density
D
A restoring tendency operates around the matching density; molecular length alone does not define band position.
B
A fully light duplex after the second light round contains:
Two strands made in that same round|One strand from its immediate parent and one newly made strand|No template-derived information|Two ancestral heavy strands
B
The immediate parent can supply an already light strand. Label history is not identical to age relative to the current round.
B
What is a replication fork?
The full chromosome|A sequence that always initiates copying|A branch-like boundary at which parental DNA is being copied|A single polymerase protein
C
The fork is a structural and functional boundary; the origin, replicon and polymerase denote different entities.
B
Which term denotes a unit of DNA duplication controlled by an initiation event?
Replicon|Codon|Promoter|Chromatid
A
A replicon can include many genes. A promoter regulates transcription; codons specify translation information.
B
A typical bidirectional initiation event generates how many active forks initially?
One|Two|Four|One per gene
B
The two copying fronts move away in opposite spatial directions, while all ordinary new DNA synthesis remains 5′→3′.
B
In the Taylor–Woods–Hughes experiment, the tracer was:
Nitrogen-15 ammonium salt|Fluorescent antibody against helicase|Radioactive thymidine|Cesium chloride
C
Tritium-labeled thymidine marks DNA synthesized during the pulse and is detected by autoradiography.
B
The relevant units compared in the plant chromosome pulse-chase experiment were primarily:
Homologous maternal and paternal chromosomes|Sister chromatids|Ribosomal subunits|Individual base pairs
B
The label is followed between sisters produced by replication; homologs are not the two products of one copying event.
B
A cis-acting replicator differs from a trans-acting initiator because:
It is necessarily a protein|It acts as an RNA polymerase|It is a local DNA element influencing initiation on its own molecule|It is a synonym for the fork
C
The replicator is local to the DNA; an initiator factor can be made elsewhere and act on suitable DNA targets.
B
A potential origin is passively copied before it fires. Which statement is correct?
It must still fire immediately|It was an actual initiation event|It necessarily caused a mutation|It need not be an active origin in that cycle
D
Potential sites need not be used. A neighboring fork can cover their DNA before they initiate.
B
Which is NOT implied by semiconservative replication?

Each ordinary daughter duplex retains a template strand|Sequence is copied by complementary templating|Two parental strands normally enter distinct products|Every chromosome contains exactly one origin
D
Strand inheritance does not specify origin number or timing.
B
A DNA bubble diagram contains two branch points. Without further temporal evidence, what can be concluded?
Both move at equal speeds|Both move in the same direction|The intermediate is branched, but activity and motion are not uniquely determined|It must be fully replicated
C
A static shape cannot distinguish two moving fronts from one moving front and a stationary or stalled boundary.
B
Which observation addresses genome completion rather than sequence fidelity most directly?
All chromosomal regions acquire duplicated copies|A polymerase rejects a mismatch|A base is corrected after misincorporation|A proofreading reaction removes a nucleotide
A
Completion concerns coverage of the genome. The other observations concern accuracy or correction.
B
When two adjacent bidirectional bubbles meet internally, how many active forks disappear at the convergence?
One|Two|Three|All forks in the genome
B
The two facing fronts finish their shared interval; outer fronts can remain active.
B
Which method provided classic evidence for the circular chromosome and branched replication intermediates in E. coli?
Taylor chromosome grain counting|Cairns DNA autoradiography|Protein electrophoresis|RNA sequencing
B
Cairns visualized long chromosome-derived DNA and theta-like intermediates. The other methods answer different questions.
B
Which statement about replication and chromosome number in ordinary diploid S phase is correct?
DNA content doubles, but chromosome-set ploidy remains diploid|Chromosome-set ploidy necessarily becomes tetraploid|DNA content remains 2C|Sister chromatids become homologous chromosomes
A
DNA content increases from 2C to 4C, while chromosome sets remain diploid until segregation.
C
A culture starts with 12 HH duplexes. After four complete light rounds, how many HL and LL duplexes exist?
B
Total = 12×16 = 192. The 24 original heavy strands each occupy a hybrid; LL = 192−24 = 168.
C
From entirely HH DNA, 3.125% of all completed duplexes are HL after a light chase. How many rounds occurred?
C
3.125% = 1/32 = 2^(1−n), so n=6. The heavy-chain fraction would be half this percentage.
C
In the preceding situation with six rounds, what percentage of all strands are originally heavy?
A
The original material fraction is 2^−6 = 1/64 = 1.5625%. Only one chain per hybrid is heavy.
C
A mixture contains 30 HH, 50 HL and 20 LL molecules. One exclusively light round occurs. What is the HL fraction?
B
Original heavy chains = 60+50=110; all now occupy hybrids among 200 duplexes, giving 55%.
C
Starting from one HH duplex, two light rounds are followed by one heavy round. What are the products?
2 HH and 6 HL|4 HH and 4 LL|2 HL and 6 LL|8 HH
A
Before the switch there are 2 HL and 2 LL. In heavy medium each HL gives HH+HL, each LL gives 2 HL.
C
In the preceding heavy-switch products, how many chains are the original heavy chains?
A
The two initial strands remain; eight newly synthesized chains are also heavy. Isotope identity does not uniquely identify genealogy.
C
Light and heavy reference densities are 1.700 and 1.716 g cm⁻³. What is the predicted uniform dispersive density after three light rounds?
A
The heavy fraction is 1/8. Under linear calibration, 1.700+0.016/8=1.702 g cm⁻³.
C
With the same calibration, which semiconservative density distribution is expected after three rounds?
B
HL is 2^(1−3)=1/4 and lies halfway between references; the remaining 3/4 is LL.
C
Two density profiles have identical mean density but one has two resolved peaks and the other one peak. Which conclusion is warranted?
They must have the same inheritance mechanism|The mean alone cannot distinguish their molecular distributions|The two-peak sample contains twice the DNA|Both are necessarily conservative
B
Different distributions can have the same weighted mean. DNA quantity and mechanism require additional information.
C

A sample has 20 HH and 80 HL molecules, all descendants of a heavy starting population after some originals completed one light round while others stayed unchanged. How many original molecules completed duplication?
B
Each copied HH contributes two HL; 80/2=40 originals completed replication. The other 20 stayed unchanged.
C
A 3.6-Mb circular DNA molecule initiates two forks at 600 bp/s each. Ideal completion time?
25 min|50 min|75 min|100 min
B
3,600,000/(1,200)=3,000 s = 50 min. The two forks collectively cover 1,200 bp/s.
C
A 900-kb circular chromosome has forks traveling at 20 and 25 kb/min. How far does the faster fork travel?
D
T=900/45=20 min; faster distance=25×20=500 kb.
C
A linear region has an origin 30 kb from one end and 90 kb from the other. Equal forks travel 3 kb/min. Completion time?
10 min|20 min|30 min|40 min
C
The arms require 10 and 30 minutes. The later finishing arm determines completion.
C
An internal origin in a 240-kb linear molecule launches left and right forks at 2 and 4 kb/min. Where should an ideal origin be to balance end arrival?
40 kb from left end|80 kb from left end|120 kb from left end|160 kb from left end
B
Let a/2=(240−a)/4. Then 2a=240−a, so a=80 kb.
C
A 40-Mb chromosome must be copied within 100 minutes at 2 kb/min per fork. Minimum ideal simultaneous symmetric bidirectional origins?
B
m≥40,000/(2×2×100)=100. Real nonuniform schedules may require more.
C
Two origins 120 kb apart fire 10 min apart. Inward forks both travel at 3 kb/min. Where do they meet relative to the first origin?
45 kb|60 kb|75 kb|90 kb
C
The first fork gains 30 kb. The remaining 90 kb is shared equally, so it covers another 45 kb and meets at 75 kb.
C
Two origins are 80 kb apart. A first fork moves at 4 kb/min; the second origin is scheduled to fire after 25 min. What is predicted under ordinary once-per-cycle control?
Both forks necessarily meet at midpoint|The second region can be passively copied before firing|The first fork cannot reach the second origin|Both origins must copy the same region twice
B
The first fork reaches the second site in 20 min, before scheduled firing. A potential origin may be passively replicated.
C
A first-label central tract is flanked by later-label tracts on both sides of an intact fiber. Which event best fits?
Two converging forks only|An outward bidirectional copying event|Conservative strand inheritance|A complete absence of replication
B
Later synthesis lies outward from earlier synthesis. The pattern supports outward progression; it does not establish strand ancestry.
C
A 15-minute pulse labels 27 kb along a single known fork. Average geometric rate?
1.8 kb/min|3.6 kb/min|27 kb/min|0.56 kb/min
A
27/15=1.8 kb/min. The 2-fold factor applies to nucleotide incorporation across both templates, not this geometric track length.
C
A mutant has shorter fiber tracks but the same measured number of initiation events as the control. Equal pulses and intact ongoing tracks are specified. What is most directly supported?
Reduced average fork progression|Loss of all replication origins|Conservative copying|Increased chromosome ploidy
A
Under the stated controls, shorter tracks imply reduced progression. The data do not uniquely identify the responsible molecular protein.
AR
Assertion: Both heavy parental chains persist after many ideal light rounds. Reason: Semiconservative copying separates and retains each parental strand while forming new complements.
Both true; reason explains assertion|Both true; reason does not explain assertion|Assertion true; reason false|Assertion false; reason true
A
Under the no-loss assumptions, each parental chain survives as a template-derived strand in one descendant.
AR
Assertion: A light-only duplex can appear after two light rounds. Reason: Light strands made during the first round become templates during the second.
Both true; reason explains assertion|Both true; reason does not explain assertion|Assertion true; reason false|Assertion false; reason true
A
A first-round light template acquires another light partner. No violation of semiconservative copying occurs.
AR
Assertion: The same density band position proves the same ancestry of every molecule. Reason: Distinct molecular arrangements can have identical average isotope composition.
Both true; reason explains assertion|Both true; reason does not explain assertion|Assertion true; reason false|Assertion false; reason true
D
Density measures composition, not unique ancestry. The reason explains why the assertion is false.
AR
Assertion: A single intermediate band after one light round uniquely proves semiconservative replication. Reason: Classical uniformly dispersive replication also predicts an intermediate band.
Both true; reason explains assertion|Both true; reason does not explain assertion|Assertion true; reason false|Assertion false; reason true
D
The first-round result eliminates simple conservative copying but does not separate the remaining two models.
AR
Assertion: All new DNA at both forks is synthesized 5′→3′. Reason: The forks necessarily move in the same spatial direction.
Both true; reason explains assertion|Both true; reason does not explain assertion|Assertion true; reason false|Assertion false; reason true
C
The synthesis direction is chemical; the two forks of a bidirectional bubble move oppositely.
MS

Select the correct statements: I. An HL duplex contains one heavy strand. II. Every LL duplex is wholly newly synthesized in the current round. III. An origin is distinct from a fork. IV. Nitrogen-15 is stable.
I and II|I, III and IV|II and IV|All four
B
II is false: an LL duplex can inherit a light template from an earlier round. The remaining statements are correct.
MS
Select the valid assumptions for T=L/(2mv): I. Equal constant fork speeds. II. Simultaneous origin activation. III. Balanced nonoverlapping replicon lengths. IV. All origins are inactive.
I, II and III|I and IV|II and III only|All four
A
The ideal time assumes simultaneous productive forks covering equal regions; inactive origins cannot contribute capacity.
MS

Which statements about autoradiography are correct? I. Tritium emits radioactive decay. II. Grain location can report labeled DNA distribution. III. Every grain identifies an individual nucleotide sequence. IV. Pulse and observation times can differ.
I, II and IV|I and III|II and III|All four
A
The method reports spatial signal at finite resolution, not individual sequence identity.
MS

Select correct statements about replicons: I. A chromosome may have multiple replicons. II. A replicon equals a gene. III. Neighboring fork convergence can establish an effective boundary. IV. Potential origins always fire.
I and III|I and IV|II and III|All four
A
The replication unit is distinct from a gene; potential sites may be passively copied.
M
Match the terms: 1. Origin; 2. Fork; 3. Replicon; 4. Bubble. P. Copied region between branch points; Q. Functional duplication unit; R. Initiation location; S. Copying boundary.
A
Each term identifies a different spatial or functional feature of replication.
revision: Strand ancestry: write the actual daughter duplexes before predicting density. For HH → light, first generation HL only; later generations HL plus LL.
Use n≥1 for fHL=2^(1−n). The fraction of originally heavy chains is 2^−n. In mixed populations, fH=fHH+fHL/2.
Band position reports buoyant density; integrated area approximates DNA quantity with suitable calibration. Equal mean densities can conceal distinct distributions.
Heat denaturation distinguishes intact heavy/light chains from a uniformly mixed chain; compare denatured reference samples.
Taylor: label both sisters in the initial complete pulse, then one sister after the chase, apart from exchanges or imperfect labeling.
Origin is a location; fork is a copying boundary; bubble is a locally copied region; replicon is a functional unit of duplication.
Bidirectional does not mean 3′→5′ synthesis. Both new strands grow 5′→3′.
Circle: T=L/(v1+v2). Linear internal origin: T=max(a/vL,b/vR). Ideal m balanced origins: T=L/(2mv).
With equal inward speeds and delay Δ, the meeting coordinate is (D+vΔ)/2 if the second origin fires before passive copying.
More than one potential origin does not guarantee that each fires; snapshots of bubbles do not count historical initiation events.
